The Clark Doll Experiment. In the 1940s, psychologists Kenneth and Mamie Clark conducted experiments that documented the psychological damage of racial segregation. They showed Black children four dolls—identical except for skin colour—and asked which doll was nice, pretty, good, and which they wanted to play with.

Most of the Black children aged three to seven preferred the white dolls. More troubling still, they attributed positive traits to the white dolls and negative traits to the Black dolls. The Clarks interpreted this as evidence of internalized racial prejudice: segregation had damaged these children's self-image and sense of worth. The children's awareness of race was sharp and their preference for whiteness was consistent, suggesting that social conditioning about race began early and ran deep.

The study's most famous moment came when it informed legal history. In 1954, the Supreme Court cited the Clark studies as evidence that "separate educational facilities are inherently unequal" in the landmark case Brown v. Board of Education, using psychology to argue for desegregation.

Yet the study was not without critics. Later researchers noted methodological limits: the samples were small, some of the questions leading, and causation unclear. Did segregation itself cause the preference, or did broader media influence and cultural messaging about race create it? The question remains debated.

Despite these limitations, the Clark Doll Experiment remains iconic. It demonstrated psychology's power to document social injustice and gave voice to what segregated Black children themselves were experiencing. Whether the mechanism was precisely what the Clarks proposed or something more complex, the harm was real and visible.
